claims.text: NiTi shape memory alloys exhibit pronounced temperature-dependent plastic deformation behavior.
The temperature dependence of NiTi deformation is caused by a reversible martensitic-to-austenitic phase transformation.
The martensitic-to-austenitic transformation alters the dominant plasticity mechanisms in NiTi.
Prior thermal treatments can establish martensitic or austenitic initial phases in NiTi.
Sub-ambient temperatures stabilize the martensitic phase in NiTi.
Elevated temperatures induce or stabilize the austenitic phase in NiTi.
The reversible phase transformation is accompanied by microstructural reorientation.
The reversible phase transformation changes dislocation mobility.
Increasing temperature transforms NiTi and modifies the energy landscape for dislocation motion and plastic flow.
Balancing slip with phase transformation enables controlled plastic deformation in NiTi.
The combination of slip and phase transformation avoids brittle failure of the type observed in conventional metals.
Crossing the martensitic-to-austenitic transformation range will produce measurable shifts in yield strength and ductility.
NiTi will show distinct plastic-deformation regimes corresponding to its martensitic and austenitic phases.
Below the transformation range, deformation is dominated by martensitic-phase behavior.
Above the transformation range, austenitic behavior prevails and produces different stress-strain characteristics.
Under isothermal room-temperature conditions with one predominant phase, NiTi shows relatively constant mechanical properties.
If thermal cycling does not cross the transformation temperatures, the predicted variation in deformation mechanisms will not occur.
Small strain-rate variations may be insufficient to produce observable effects on dislocation kinetics.
The hypothesis is falsified if mechanical properties remain invariant across a temperature range that crosses the phase-transformation temperatures.
